'''Juliane Margaret Beate Koepcke''' (born 10 October 1954) is a German-Peruvian [[mammalogy|mammalogist]] who specialises in [[bat]]s. She is the daughter of German zoologists [[Maria Koepcke|Maria]] and [[Hans-Wilhelm Koepcke]].

Koepcke is known for being the [[List of aviation accidents and incidents with a sole survivor|sole survivor]] of the 1971 [[LANSA Flight 508]] crash. When the plane was struck by lightning, she fell {{cvt|3000|m|ft|sigfig=1}} while strapped to her seat and suffered numerous injuries including a concussion, broken collarbone, and a torn knee ligament. She survived 11 days alone in the Peruvian [[Amazon rainforest]] until she located a lumberjack camp.

== Early life ==
Koepcke was born in [[Lima]], Peru, on 10 October 1954, the only child of German zoologists [[Maria Koepcke|Maria]] (née von Mikulicz-Radecki; 1924–1971) and [[Hans-Wilhelm Koepcke]] (1914–2000). Her parents were working at Lima's [[Museum of Natural History, Lima|Museum of Natural History]] when she was born. At the age of 14, she left Lima with her parents to establish the [[Panguana]] research station in the [[Amazon rainforest]], where she learned [[survival skills]]. Educational authorities disapproved and she was required to return to the [[Deutsche Schule Lima Alexander von Humboldt]] to take her examinations, graduating on 23 December 1971.<ref name=telegraph>{{cite web |url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/authorinterviews/9143701/Sole-survivor-the-woman-who-fell-to-earth.html |title= Sole survivor: the woman who fell to earth |first= Sally |last= Williams |website= The Telegraph |date= 22 March 2012}}</ref>

== Plane crash ==
On 24 December 1971, just one day after she graduated, Koepcke flew on [[LANSA Flight 508]]. Her mother Maria had wanted Juliane to return to Panguana with her on 19 or 20 December, but Koepcke wanted to attend her graduation ceremony in Lima on 23 December. Maria agreed that they would stay for her graduation and instead they scheduled a flight for [[Christmas Eve]]. All flights were fully booked except for one with [[Líneas Aéreas Nacionales S.A.|LANSA]]. Koepcke's father, Hans-Wilhelm, urged his wife to avoid flying with the airline due to its poor reputation.<ref name="telegraph" /> Nonetheless, the flight was booked. The plane was struck by lightning mid-flight and began to disintegrate before plummeting to the ground. Koepcke found herself falling, still strapped to her row of seats,  {{cvt|3000|m|ft|sigfig=1}} into the Amazon rainforest.

Koepcke survived the fall but suffered injuries including a [[Clavicle fracture|broken collarbone]], a deep cut on her right arm, an eye injury, a ruptured ligament in her knee, and a [[concussion]]. She then spent 11 days in the rainforest, most of which she spent following a creek to a river. While in the jungle, she dealt with severe insect bites and an infestation of [[botfly]] larvae in her injured arm. After nine days, she was able to find an encampment that had been set up by local lumberjacks. A few hours later, the returning lumberjacks found her, poured gasoline onto her wound, and used a canoe to transport her for 11 hours to a more inhabited area. She was then airlifted to a hospital.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Koepcke |first1=Juliane |title=When I Fell From the Sky |date=2011 |publisher=TitleTown Publishing |location=Green Bay, WI |isbn=978-0-9837547-0-1 |page=67 |edition= 1st English}}</ref>

Koepcke's unlikely survival has been the subject of much speculation. Experts have said that she survived the fall because she was harnessed into her seat, the window seat, which was attached to the two seats to her left as part of a row of three. That was thought to have functioned as a parachute or helicopter which slowed her fall.<ref name="CNN">{{cite news |date=2 July 2009 |title=Survivor still haunted by 1971 air crash |publisher=CNN.com |url=http://www.cnn.com/2009/WORLD/europe/07/02/germany.aircrash.survivor/index.html |url-status=dead |access-date=30 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180225140559/http://www.cnn.com/2009/WORLD/europe/07/02/germany.aircrash.survivor/index.html |archive-date=25 February 2018}}</ref><ref name=Natura>{{Cite web |url=http://www.naturapop.com/home/the-incredible-fall-of-juliane-koepcke |title=The incredible fall of Juliane Koepcke |author=Loup, Aldo |date=2013 |publisher=Natura Pop |work=Naturapop.com |access-date=16 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130518072049/http://www.naturapop.com/home/the-incredible-fall-of-juliane-koepcke |archive-date=18 May 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The impact may have also been lessened by the [[vertical draft|updraft]] from a thunderstorm Koepcke fell through, as well as the thick foliage at her landing site.<ref name="CNN"/><ref name=Natura/> As many as 14 other passengers were later discovered to have survived the initial crash but died while waiting to be rescued.<ref>{{Cite web |title=17-Year-Old Only Survivor in Peruvian Accident |url=http://www.super70s.com/Super70s/Tech/Aviation/Disasters/71-12-24(Lansa).asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170508023054/http://www.super70s.com/Super70s/Tech/Aviation/Disasters/71-12-24(Lansa).asp |archive-date=8 May 2017}}</ref>

== Aftermath ==
{{quote box |width=30% |quote=I had nightmares for a long time, for years, and of course the grief about my mother's death and that of the other people came back again and again. The thought "why was I the only survivor?" haunts me. It always will. |author=Koepcke in 2010<ref name=Harpers11>{{Cite magazine |last1=Littlewood |first1=Tom |date=January 2011 |title=After the Fall |magazine=Harper's |publisher=Harper's Foundation |volume=322 |issue=1,928 |pages=20–23 |url=http://harpers.org/archive/2011/01/0083244 |access-date=29 July 2011}}</ref> |salign=right}}
After recovering from her injuries, Koepcke assisted search parties in locating the crash site and recovering the bodies of victims. Her mother's body was discovered on 12 January 1972.

Koepcke returned to her parents' native West Germany, where she fully recovered from her physical injuries. Like her parents, she studied [[biology]] at the [[University of Kiel]] and graduated in 1980.<ref name=HWKobit>{{cite journal |url= http://sora.unm.edu/node/119463 |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages= 215–218 |title=Hans-Wilhelm Koepcke |first=Francois |last= Vuilleumier |journal= Ornitologia Neotropical |date=2002}}</ref> She received a doctorate from [[LMU Munich]] and returned to Peru to conduct research in [[mammalogy]], specialising in bats.<ref name=HWKobit/> She published her thesis, "Ecological study of a bat colony in the tropical rain forest of Peru", in 1987.<ref>{{cite book |first=Juliane |last= Koepcke |title=Ökologische Studien an einer Fledermaus-Artengemeinschaft im tropischen Regenwald von Peru |language= de |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=Bt17HAAACAAJ |oclc=230848237 |year=1987}}</ref>

In 1989, Koepcke married Erich Diller, a German entomologist who specialises in parasitic wasps.<ref name="NYT">{{cite news |last1=Lidz |first1=Franz |title=She Fell Nearly 2 Miles, and Walked Away |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/18/science/koepcke-diller-panguana-amazon-crash.html |work=The New York Times |date=18 June 2021}}</ref> In 2000, following the death of her father, she took over as the director of [[Panguana]].<ref name="NYT" /> She served as a librarian at the [[Bavarian State Collection of Zoology]] in [[Munich]].<ref name="CNN"/>

Koepcke's autobiography ''Als ich vom Himmel fiel: Wie mir der Dschungel mein Leben zurückgab'' (German for ''When I Fell from the Sky: How the Jungle Gave Me My Life Back'') was released in 2011 by [[Piper Verlag]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Diller, Juliane |author2=Rygiert, Beate |title=Als ich vom Himmel fiel: Wie mir der Dschungel mein Leben zurückgab |trans-title= When I fell from the sky: How the jungle gave me my life back |language= de |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=ZZRfywAACAAJ|date=2011 |publisher=Malik|isbn=978-3-89029-389-9}}</ref> The book won that year's [[Corine Literature Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.corine.de/chronik/index.php |title=Corine Internationaler Buchpreis |date=2013 |publisher=National Exchange Association of Bavaria |work=Corine.de |language= de |access-date=16 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029201013/http://www.corine.de/chronik/index.php |archive-date=29 October 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2019, the government of Peru made her a Grand Officer of the Order of Merit for Distinguished Services.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.gob.pe/institucion/rree/noticias/27182-condecoran-a-juliane-koepcke-por-su-labor-cientifica-y-academica-en-la-amazonia-peruana |title=Condecoran a Juliane Koepcke por su labor científica y académica en la Amazonía peruana |access-date=19 August 2019 |website= gob.pe |language= es |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190819093740/https://www.gob.pe/institucion/rree/noticias/27182-condecoran-a-juliane-koepcke-por-su-labor-cientifica-y-academica-en-la-amazonia-peruana |archive-date=19 August 2019 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Portrayal in media ==
Koepcke's survival has been the subject of numerous books and films, including the low-budget and heavily fictionalized ''I miracoli accadono ancora'' (1974) by Italian filmmaker [[Giuseppe Maria Scotese]], which was released in English as ''[[Miracles Still Happen]]'' and is sometimes called ''The Story of Juliane Koepcke''. She was portrayed by English actress [[Susan Penhaligon]] in the film.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0071845/ |title=IMDb: The Story of Juliane Koepcke (1975) |date=2011 |publisher=Internet Movie Database |access-date=29 July 2011}}</ref>

Koepcke's story was more faithfully told by Koepcke herself in German filmmaker [[Werner Herzog]]'s documentary ''[[Wings of Hope (film)|Wings of Hope]]'' (1998). Herzog was interested in telling her story because of a personal connection: He was scheduled to be on the same flight while scouting locations for his film ''[[Aguirre, the Wrath of God]]'' (1972), but a last-minute change of plans spared him from the crash.<ref name="hh">{{cite book |last= Herzog |first= Werner |title= Herzog on Herzog |publisher= [[Faber and Faber]] |date= 2001 |isbn= 0-571-20708-1 |url-access= registration |url= https://archive.org/details/herzogonherzog00herz}}</ref> He had planned to make the film ever since narrowly missing the flight but was unable to contact Koepcke for decades because she avoided the media; he located her after contacting the priest who performed her mother's funeral.<ref name="hh" /> Koepcke accompanied him on a visit to the crash site, which she described as a "kind of therapy" for her.<ref>Banister interview, 24:20.</ref>

[[Franz Lidz]] described Koepcke as one of his most interesting interview subjects,<ref name="t431">{{cite web |last=Lidz |first=Franz |date=2021-06-18 |title=She Fell Nearly 2 Miles, and Walked Away |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/18/science/koepcke-diller-panguana-amazon-crash.html |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=The New York Times}}</ref> noting that she was initially reluctant to participate, until Lidz convinced her he "just wanted to write about the science of it, rather than focusing on the childhood trauma".<ref name="u168">{{cite web |last=Bahr |first=Sarah |date=2025-09-26 |title=A Writer Who Delights in Demystifying the Arcane and Obscure |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/26/insider/franz-lidz.html |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=The New York Times}}</ref>
